Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

vignette: Luis, a 26‑year‑old man of Mexican heritage, was forced into a small, cramped vehicle by guards during a nighttime raid in his hometown. The car’s interior smelled of sweat and fear; the driver’s hands shook as he clamped a blindfold over Luis’s eyes and drove for hours. When the car finally stopped, the guards pulled Luis out, bruised and gagged, and began a session of verbal and physical torture that lasted three days. The memory of that car—its color, its cramped interior, the constant hiss of the engine—has since become a living echo of that terror. After the trauma, Luis’s nights were haunted. One night he heard the distant rumble of a truck and immediately felt a surge of panic, as if the car were returning. The sound triggered a flashback, and his heart rate spiked. He woke with a jolt, convinced that someone was near, and checked whether he was safe, only to find the apartment dark and silent. That sense of threat—his body’s rapid response to a mundane sound—became a constant backdrop to his day. The very act of waking to assess safety fed into the same pattern, and when he returned to bed he found the darkness itself frightening. The loop was relentless: the trigger of a car’s hum produced a threat response, which in turn amplified the perception of threat, prompting Luis to take the next step. Luis’s response to these moments was to avoid anything that might remind him of the car. He stayed away from street corners where traffic lights blinked like the guard’s gloved fingers, and he resisted conversations that touched on cars, even if his friend asked about a new vehicle. His avoidance was not limited to the physical environment; he steered clear of authority figures—a police officer’s uniform, a supervisor’s badge—because the very sight of them reminded him of the guards. Each time a reminder arose, he would pull out his pack of cigarettes, lighting one in the hallway to numb the rising dread. The smoking became a ritual of comfort, but it also amplified his sense of threat, because the cough and the flash of the flame echoed the grim flashbacks he tried to outrun. His avoidance of reminders, avoidance of authority, and smoking each fed back into the cycle, tightening the loop. When a neighbor passed by with a delivery truck, Luis felt an immediate surge of threat, and he could not help but think that the vehicle was a prelude to another round of torture. The trigger had re‑ignited the same pattern of threat and avoidance. The consequence of this cycle was a decline in his work as a maid. Luis worked late hours at an elderly woman’s house, but the woman’s son—an orderly man in a security guard’s vest—often asked him to move furniture. The sight of the uniform sparked Luis’s anxiety, so he would stall, mumbling that he was “not sure” about the move. The woman’s son grew frustrated; the woman’s family began to distance themselves from Luis, leaving him to clean the house alone. His smoking habit also took a toll on his health; he developed a sore throat that required a doctor's visit, and he began to dread even his routine visits to the clinic, fearing that the waiting room’s fluorescent lights would trigger a flashback. The work environment, once a source of routine, became a minefield of triggers, threats, and maladaptive coping. After a month of escalating irritability and frequent night awakenings, Luis finally decided to seek help. He realized that each time he avoided a trigger, the threat felt larger; each time he smoked to soothe the threat, the sense of danger deepened. The constant cycle was draining his energy and his relationships. He feared that if he stayed the same, he would lose his job and become isolated, but he also feared the pain that might come from confronting the memories head‑on. His most immediate hope was to break the loop and find relief from the nightly checks, the panic at a passing truck, and the dread of authority figures—so he could return to a life that did not revolve around survival.
